reason: Jo's question points directly to placing the rider on the moving cord to observe what travels.
expectation: The rider will show how the cord moves as the wiggle passes.

effect: The rider shows that the disturbance travels while a point on the cord mainly moves around its own place. Next I can explore how adjusting the cord affects the wave.
reaction: The distinction between the moving wave and the bobbing rider is satisfying.
reason: The tension-adjusting key looks useful for changing how the cord behaves.

choice.with: Wave cord with a paper rider

expectation: Adjusting the tension will change the visible wave.

effect: Adjusting tension and speed produced a standing pattern with two loops and a nearly still point. I can now try setting up the cord to play it like a string.
reaction: Seeing opposite-travelling disturbances make a stationary pattern is intriguing.
reason: The movable bridge seems like the next part for turning the cord into a playable string.
expectation: The bridge will support the cord and establish a playable length.

effect: The bridge changes the vibrating length and transfers vibration to the soundbox; the cord is now ready for further preparation or playing.
reaction: The connection between the bridge, wave pattern and soundbox is interesting.
reason: The plectrum is the obvious tool for testing the cord as a string.

choice.with: Cord resting on a movable bridge

expectation: Plucking the cord will make it vibrate and produce a sound.

choice.with: Cord resting on a movable bridge

alternatives.reason: The pads may need to be fitted before playing.

effect: The plectrum has no available operation yet, so the string likely needs further preparation.
reaction: The failed test is a little frustrating, but the remaining pads offer a clear next step.
reason: The foot pads are the remaining unfitted part and may prepare the machine for playing.

choice.with: Cord resting on a movable bridge

expectation: The pads will fit to the machine and help prepare it for the sound test.

effect: The pads reduced table buzz while leaving the cord moving, and the drive is now off for the instrument test.
reaction: It is useful to see why the pads matter; I tried the plectrum too early.
reason: The machine is now prepared for the sound test, so I can retry the plectrum.
expectation: Plucking the cord will make it vibrate and produce a sound.

effect: The finished test showed that shortening the vibrating length raises the note, and that the machine can return to its broad wave pattern.
reaction: The comparison between the visible loops and the audible notes was satisfying.

mostWorthwhile.text: Plucking the cord and moving the bridge was most worthwhile: it connected a physical adjustment to a clearly different note.

leastWorthwhile.text: The failed early plectrum attempt was the least worthwhile moment; it did not explain what preparation was missing.

surprise.text: The paper rider bobbed in place while the disturbance travelled along the cord, making the distinction between the wave and the cord tangible.

arbitrary.text: The need to fit the soft feet before plucking initially felt arbitrary, though the subsequent reduction in table buzz gave them a clear purpose.

continue.text: Yes. Comparing the standing loops with the string's changing notes made me curious about what another construction might demonstrate.
